en: On Sunday I went to the mountains with my father and mother. We left home early in the morning and rode the train for about an hour. From the top of the mountain we could see a river and a small town. The sky was high and it felt wonderful. For lunch we ate the packed lunch my mother had made. It was delicious. en: There was a time when I thought it was better to read quickly. I counted how many books I read in a year and believed the more the better. But last winter, when I was ill and rested for about a week, that view changed. With nothing else to do, I read the same book over and over. Words I had not noticed the first time became visible on the second and third readings. It is the same text, yet what I feel differs each time I read it. Now I have stopped counting. I have come to think that meeting a single line that stays in your heart matters far more than reading fast.

r: でもできるようになった。

She does not carry a phone.

p.e: The shopkeeper then tells her a shortcut not on any map, or recommends somewhere cheap and good to eat.

en: These days you can do almost anything with a phone. If you lose your way, a map tells you; a word you do not know can be looked up on the spot. It is certainly convenient. But for all that convenience, is there not something we have lost? Once, you asked someone the way to the station. You looked at their face and thanked them. Now there is no need. Walk while watching the screen and you arrive. It is faster, but there is no contact with another person in it. I noticed this while travelling with my grandmother. She does not carry a phone. When she loses her way she goes into a nearby shop and asks. The shopkeeper then tells her a shortcut not on any map, or recommends somewhere cheap and good to eat. It was far richer than the information I got by looking things up. There is no need to throw the convenient tools away. But if we come to rely on them entirely, we may overlook what we could in fact have had.

p.e: As a child, I was afraid of failing.

r: えると、はずかしかったからだ。

r: しながら、しんちょうに

r: したほどよくなかった。
p.e: But the result was not as good as I had hoped.

r: は、わたしとはちがった。
p.e: The colleague at the next desk, who joined when I did, was different from me.
She tried things as soon as she thought of them, and changed her approach the moment she saw it was not working.
She failed far more often than I did, but in the end she produced a good result.

r: はどこにあったのだろう。
p.e: Where did that difference lie?
I thought of failure as something to avoid; she thought of it as something to find early.

r: かすかなのだと、そのとき
p.e: What matters is not the number of failures but what you learn from them and how quickly you put it to use — that was when I first realised it.

en: As a child I was afraid of failing. If I raised my hand and got the answer wrong, it was embarrassing. So I only raised my hand for questions I was certain about. After I started working, that view changed. When I was given a new job, I went about it carefully, checking over and over so as never to fail once. But the result was not as good as I had hoped. The colleague who joined at the same time, sitting next to me, was different. She tried things as soon as she thought of them, and changed her approach the moment she saw it was not working. She failed far more often than I did, yet in the end she produced the better result. Where did that difference lie? I thought of failure as something to avoid; she thought of it as something to find early. What matters is not the number of failures but what you learn from them and how quickly you put it to use. That was when I first realised it.

en: People sometimes say that young people's language is deteriorating. Each time they hear a new expression, many worry that correct Japanese is being lost. But language has always been changing. Among expressions now regarded as correct there are many that were once criticised as errors. Seen that way, it is hardly fair to treat only today's changes as a special problem. That said, it does not follow that every change should be accepted. The role of language is to convey your thoughts to the other person accurately. If you use wording that only works among friends with someone you have just met, or with a senior, it may not only fail to get through but leave them uncomfortable. What matters, surely, is not stopping change but acquiring the ability to use language differently according to the person and the situation.

p.e: It has become normal for what you order to arrive the next day.

r: くのはありがたいが、そのせいで

en: It has become normal for what you order to arrive the next day. Fast delivery is welcome, but it seems to me something has been lost because of it. As a child, when I asked my father for a book it took about two weeks to arrive. During that time I imagined the cover over and over — what picture was on it, how it would feel in my hands. The joy when it actually arrived was, I think, held up by the length of time I had spent imagining. And now? The box arrives the day after you order, you open it, check it, and that is that. With no time before getting it, the feeling after getting it is somehow thinner too. I have no intention of giving up convenience. But in a life where anything can be had at once, we may be slowly forgetting the richness that waiting used to give us.

ti: 子どもにけいたい電話を持たせるか

p.e: A.

r: しかし、だからといって
ることになるだろうか。

p.e: Even for things they could have worked out with a little thought, they would come and ask “how should I do this?”

r: げてしまっていたのだ。

r: えず、「あなたならどうしますか」と
p.e: When a question came, instead of answering at once I would ask back, “what would you do?”

r: をしていたが、やがて「たぶんこうだと
きにくるようになった。

I had thought teaching meant handing over answers.
But what really ought to be handed over is the ability to start moving where there is no answer.
For that, the one teaching has to wait a little.
Waiting is far harder than teaching.

en: When I was put in charge of training a new member of staff, I tried to teach everything carefully. I prepared a sheet setting out the steps in detail and told them to come and ask whenever anything was unclear. They listened well and worked through each task accurately. For the first few months it seemed to be going well. But after about six months something began to bother me. Whenever a situation arose that was not on the sheet, they froze. Even for things they could have worked out with a little thought, they would come and ask “how should I do this?” I would answer, and they would do exactly that. Accurate, but with no trace anywhere of their own judgement. The cause lay not with them but with me. In trying to keep the time they spent not knowing as short as possible, I had taken away the chance to think along with it. So I changed my approach. When a question came, instead of answering at once I would ask back, “what would you do?” At first they looked troubled, but before long they began coming with their own view attached: “I think it is probably this.” Sometimes they were wrong, but on those occasions their understanding after my explanation was deeper. I had thought teaching meant handing over answers. But what really ought to be handed over is the ability to start moving where there is no answer. For that, the one teaching has to wait a little. Waiting is far harder than teaching.

en:

p.e: Email is fast.

r: えればはじめからやり

During that interval, the writer goes on thinking about the person.
The receiver senses it too.
When they open the envelope, they are receiving the time spent on it along with the words.

r: えたいことはメールで
p.e: Anything you want to convey quickly can go by email.

en:
Email is fast. You write when it occurs to you and send it at once, and the other person can read it whenever suits them. It is a useful tool.
Does that mean letters are no longer needed? I do not think so. A letter contains time that email does not.
You choose the paper, take out the pen, and start again from the beginning if you make a mistake. Even when you have finished, it does not arrive at once. During that interval, the writer goes on thinking about the person.
The receiver senses it too. When they open the envelope, they are receiving the time spent on it along with the words.
Anything you want to convey quickly can go by email. But when what you want to convey is the very fact that you spent time, nothing yet matches a letter.

ti: 図書館は何を置くべきか

p.e: A.
Some people object to libraries buying many copies of popular books.
But if you have to wait half a year to borrow the book you want, fewer people will come to the library at all.
Surely getting them through the door comes first.
Someone who starts visiting because of a popular book may in time reach for a volume at the back of the shelves.

r: くすることは、けっしてむだではない。
p.e: Widening the entrance is by no means wasted effort.
B.
Line up many copies of the same book and you cannot buy other books with that money.
Popular books can be had in bookshops, and wait a little and your turn comes round anyway.
What only a library can hold is the book that does not sell but is needed.

r: らすことより、ほかのどこにもない
p.e: The role of a public library lies, I think, in keeping the one volume that exists nowhere else, rather than in reducing the number of people waiting.

en:
A. Some people object to libraries buying many copies of popular books. But if you have to wait half a year to borrow the book you want, fewer people will come to the library at all. Surely getting them through the door comes first. Someone who starts visiting because of a popular book may in time reach for a volume at the back of the shelves. Widening the entrance is by no means wasted effort.
B. Line up many copies of the same book and you cannot buy other books with that money. Popular books can be had in bookshops, and wait a little and your turn comes round anyway. What only a library can hold is the book that does not sell but is needed. The role of a public library lies, I think, in keeping the one volume that exists nowhere else, rather than in reducing the number of people waiting.

p.e: My grandfather was a man who repaired anything that broke.
If a chair leg wobbled he looked underneath; if a clock stopped he opened the back.

r: どものわたしには、それがふしぎな
p.e: To me as a child it looked like a strange kind of power.
Having grown up and become able to fix a few things myself, I have understood something.

r: っていたわけではない。
p.e: It was not that my grandfather had special skill.

r: うかどうかがちがっていたのだ。
p.e: It was that, faced with something broken, what differed was whether “maybe this can be fixed” was the first thought.

r: わたしたちは、こわれたものを
p.e: When we see something broken, we first look up the price of a new one.
We pass by the existence of repair as an option before we have considered it.
That difference is not skill but order.
Of course, some things cannot be repaired.
Often buying is cheaper than fixing, too.
Even so, look inside once.
Whether or not you have that habit changes a great deal about how you live with the things around you.
My grandfather's toolbox is in my room now.
There is nothing special in it.
What was in it, I now think, was the habit of opening things up.

en:
My grandfather was a man who repaired anything that broke. If a chair leg wobbled he looked underneath; if a clock stopped he opened the back. To me as a child it looked like a strange kind of power.
Having grown up and become able to fix a few things myself, I have understood something. It was not that my grandfather had special skill. It was that, faced with something broken, what differed was whether “maybe this can be fixed” was the first thought.
When we see something broken, we first look up the price of a new one. We pass by the existence of repair as an option before we have considered it. That difference is not skill but order.
Of course some things cannot be repaired, and often buying is cheaper than fixing. Even so, look inside once. Whether or not you have that habit changes a great deal about how you live with the things around you.
My grandfather's toolbox is in my room now. There is nothing special in it. What was in it, I now think, was the habit of opening things up.

They say you should go to the shop in the evening when buying shoes, because feet swell and are larger in the evening than in the morning.
If you choose to fit your morning size, they become tight by the end of the day and walking becomes painful. A little room is in the end less tiring.
If you decide on looks alone, you end up with shoes you bought and then barely wore.

When someone is going to be late for a meeting, they sometimes say “I'll be there in five minutes.” In fact it often takes fifteen.
The person running late wants to believe they will arrive soon, and that hope comes out of their mouth as a number.
What matters to the person waiting is not a small number but an accurate one. If it is going to take fifteen minutes, being told fifteen at the outset means they can read a book or deal with something else.

en:
Even if you decide to start saving, trying to save what is left over usually does not last, because at the end of the month there is usually nothing left over.
People who manage it do it the other way round. On payday they move a set amount into another account first. They then live on what remains — and oddly, it turns out to be enough.
Rather than relying on willpower to keep it up, building the arrangement at the start is in the end easier.

en:
At school sports days the winning and losing was clear. You competed on speed, the winning team was delighted and the losing team frustrated. I thought that was simply how things were.
When I grew up and started working, it looked different. Rather than fighting over the same piece of work, there were many situations where dividing it by what each person was good at produced a better result. At first this change confused me.
Thinking it over, competition had not disappeared. The opponent had changed. Instead of deciding who wins against the person beside you, you compete with things that are hard to see — last year's self, a deadline, the market.
The competition of running hard and coming first, and the competition of joining forces to finish by a deadline. Both require effort, but the kind of strength needed is, I now think, quite different.

p.e: My mother hardly ever looks at a cookbook.

When I asked how, she laughed and brought out an old notebook.
Opening it, there was the date she made it, the amounts of the ingredients, and the weather that day.
Short notes like “extend the steaming by two minutes” or “reduce the sugar slightly” had piled up over years.

r: そのものではなかった。
p.e: What my mother remembered was not the taste itself.

Because the failures remain rather than vanishing, she does not stumble in the same place.
This is surely not limited to cooking.
People who keep at something are strong, I think, less because they kept at it for long than because of how many times they corrected course while doing so.

en:
My mother hardly ever looks at a cookbook. Even so, however many times she makes the same cake, the taste does not change. When I asked how, she laughed and brought out an old notebook.
Opening it, there was the date she made it, the amounts of the ingredients, and the weather that day. Short notes like “extend the steaming by two minutes” or “reduce the sugar slightly” had piled up over years.
What my mother remembered was not the taste itself. It was the record of what she had changed, and how, on the days it had not gone well. Because the failures remain rather than vanishing, she does not stumble in the same place.
This is surely not limited to cooking. People who keep at something are strong, I think, less because they kept at it for long than because of how many times they corrected course while doing so.

p.e: At university I was in the drama society.
I joined wanting to act, but my body was stiff and my voice did not carry, and in the first year I was moved behind the scenes.
To be honest, it stung.
I was put in charge of the lighting.
Which lights to bring down, and how far, in which scene — you read the script closely and decide.
At first I simply moved my hands as instructed.
What changed things was the day I tried delaying a light by one second in a certain scene.
The time the actor stood there in silence grew very slightly longer.
That alone changed the air in the auditorium.
The sound of an indrawn breath reached me, backstage.
That was when I first understood.
It is not only the actors who make a performance.
The lights, the sound, the raising and lowering of the curtain.
Each of them changes how the watcher's mind moves.
The audience's eyes are on the actors, but the scene in front of those eyes is made together with the people behind.
I graduated and moved to a different job, but the experience has stayed with me.
In any setting there are people who stand at the front and people who support from out of sight.

r: めてしまうことがある。
p.e: And a small judgement by the one supporting can decide the impression of the whole.
Being noticed and having an effect are two different things.

en:
At university I was in the drama society. I joined wanting to act, but my body was stiff and my voice did not carry, and in the first year I was moved behind the scenes. To be honest, it stung.
I was put in charge of lighting — reading the script closely to decide which lights to bring down, how far, and in which scene. At first I simply moved my hands as instructed.
What changed things was the day I tried delaying a light by one second in a certain scene. The time the actor stood there in silence grew very slightly longer. That alone changed the air in the auditorium. The sound of an indrawn breath reached me, backstage.
That was when I first understood. It is not only the actors who make a performance. The lights, the sound, the raising and lowering of the curtain — each changes how the watcher's mind moves. The audience's eyes are on the actors, but the scene in front of those eyes is made together with the people behind.
I graduated and took a different job, but the experience has stayed with me. In any setting there are people who stand at the front and people who support from out of sight. And a small judgement by the one supporting can decide the impression of the whole.
Being noticed and having an effect are two different things.

p.e: Feeling that you have stopped is, more often than not, simply progress having grown small enough not to rise into awareness.
A record puts that small progress into visible form, and joins it up with your next preparation.

en:
When you are practising something, there comes a point where you suddenly stop feeling any improvement. It is not that your ability has fallen, yet you end up in a state of going round and round the same spot.
This is where most people want to change their method. They buy a book with a new way of teaching, look for a different teacher, and start again from the first chapter. But the moment you change, what had been accumulating in the body until then can end up never being used.
What I would recommend is to keep a record before changing your method. Write just one line about what you managed today. Keep that up for a month, and a difference of degree you had not noticed yourself appears on the paper.
Research says that people judge their own rate of progress to be lower than it is. Feeling that you have stopped is, more often than not, simply progress having grown small enough not to rise into awareness. A record puts that small progress into visible form, and joins it up with your next preparation.

p.e: Resting tends to be thought of as doing nothing.

p.e: This is said to be because the brain has not stopped working.

You sleep better at night after a day of moving your arms and legs a little and getting a few light errands out of the way.
The older you get, the larger this difference becomes.

r: くのがつらくなって、さらに

Rather than stopping completely, make a day on which you move at half your usual speed.

en:
Resting tends to be thought of as doing nothing. But there are days when you have lain down all day and by evening your body feels heavier instead.
This is said to be because the brain has not stopped working. It seems that if too little comes in from outside, the human brain becomes unsettled. You sleep better at night after a day of moving your arms and legs a little and getting a few light errands out of the way.
The older you get, the larger this difference becomes. Bones and muscles weaken quickly when they are not used, and once they weaken, moving becomes hard, so they are used even less.
Rather than stopping completely, make a day on which you move at half your usual speed. That is what a day of rest means to me.

p.e: A.

p.e: Last autumn I walked around a small village at the end of a railway line.
It was because the village had been described in a book my friend's name appears on as author.
Coming out of the station, fields and a wood opened out at once, with forest and mountains in the distance.
The road ran down towards the river, with an old wooden bridge partway along.

r: くなるまでかわいていて、
p.e: The planks of the bridge had dried until they were white, and they gave a low sound as I walked.
At the centre of the village stood a temple, and beside it a small shrine hall.
In front of the hall lay flowers made of Japanese paper.
What surprised me was not how old the buildings were.
It was that the way of keeping the old form was not the same formula everywhere.

r: のままのかべをそのまま
p.e: One house uses its original walls as they are.
Another has rebuilt the same form out of new materials.
Yet another has left only the side visible from outside as it was, and changed the inside to suit life today.
It is not a question of which is right, a villager told me.

r: すことじゃないんです。」
p.e: "Keeping something is not the same as capturing it in a photograph."
"Once the people living here are gone, what good is the form on its own?"

r: われてみれば、そのとおりだった。
p.e: Put like that, he was right.
An old town looks beautiful because life carries on in it, not because the old form is beautiful in itself.
As I left the village, looking down at the water from the bridge, fallen leaves were drifting past.
This bridge too will be made new one day.

r: ったことになるのだと
p.e: Even so, I thought, if this village goes on being a village, that will count as having kept it.

en:
Last autumn I walked around a small village at the end of a railway line. It was because the village had been described in a book my friend's name appears on as author.
Coming out of the station, fields and a wood opened out at once, with forest and mountains in the distance. The road ran down towards the river, with an old wooden bridge partway along. The planks of the bridge had dried until they were white, and they gave a low sound as I walked. At the centre of the village stood a temple, and beside it a small shrine hall. In front of the hall lay flowers made of Japanese paper.
What surprised me was not how old the buildings were. It was that the way of keeping the old form was not the same formula everywhere. One house uses its original walls as they are. Another has rebuilt the same form out of new materials. Yet another has left only the side visible from outside as it was, and changed the inside to suit life today.
It is not a question of which is right, a villager told me. "Keeping something is not the same as capturing it in a photograph." "Once the people living here are gone, what good is the form on its own?" Put like that, he was right. An old town looks beautiful because life carries on in it, not because the old form is beautiful in itself.
As I left the village, looking down at the water from the bridge, fallen leaves were drifting past. This bridge too will be made new one day. Even so, I thought, if this village goes on being a village, that will count as having kept it.

p.e: Listening to someone's troubles is difficult.

r: えなければならないような
p.e: It is because you start to feel you have to give them something.
Finish without having produced a single answer and you feel you were no use.
But what the other person wants is, more often than not, not an answer.
When a friend was suffering over work, I offered three or so ideas.
None of them was bad, I think.
But my friend's face did not clear.

r: べられると、よけいにつらい」と
p.e: Asking later, I was told, "Having things I already know lined up for me only makes it harder."
What I had done then was not to enter her world but to introduce my own thinking.
When we try to help someone, we tend to put something in between.
Speaking through words borrowed from books or other people is safe, but it does not reach the other person.
It is precisely when you are asked for advice that you should not hurry to an answer.

r: しておくことではなく、
えをしておくことなのだろう。
p.e: Listening to someone is probably not a matter of having an answer ready, but of being ready to spend a stretch of time together in which there is no answer.
Perhaps the power to listen is decided by whether you can hold a stretch of time without exchanging words.

r: わずにいることができず、すぐに「それなら」と
p.e: Being unable to stay silent and blurting out "in that case" is not for the other person's sake but because you yourself are uneasy.
That becomes possible, I think, only when you are not trying to change the other person.
When I was a child, there was someone who sat beside me while I cried and said nothing.

r: るのは、こわいことでもある。
p.e: Taking another person's time just as it is can be frightening.

r: それでも、そうしてもらえた
p.e: Even so, anyone who has had that done for them is sure to remember it.
That although nothing had been solved, the walk home felt a little lighter.

en:
Listening to someone's troubles is difficult. It is because you start to feel you have to give them something. Finish without having produced a single answer and you feel you were no use. But what the other person wants is, more often than not, not an answer.
When a friend was suffering over work, I offered three or so ideas. None of them was bad, I think. But my friend's face did not clear. Asking later, I was told, "Having things I already know lined up for me only makes it harder." What I had done then was not to enter her world but to introduce my own thinking.
When we try to help someone, we tend to put something in between. Speaking through words borrowed from books or other people is safe, but it does not reach the other person. It is precisely when you are asked for advice that you should not hurry to an answer.
Listening to someone is probably not a matter of having an answer ready, but of being ready to spend a stretch of time together in which there is no answer. Perhaps the power to listen is decided by whether you can hold a stretch of time without exchanging words. Being unable to stay silent and blurting out "in that case" is not for the other person's sake but because you yourself are uneasy. That becomes possible, I think, only when you are not trying to change the other person.
When I was a child, there was someone who sat beside me while I cried and said nothing. Taking another person's time just as it is can be frightening. Even so, anyone who has had that done for them is sure to remember it. That although nothing had been solved, the walk home felt a little lighter.

r: がってくることはなくなった。
p.e: Thanks to it, the water no longer rises even in sudden rain.

p.e: But since the wall went up, the river cannot be seen from the town.

en:
The town I grew up in was right beside a large river. The water supported the life of the town, but the same water sometimes wrecked it.
When I was a child, the water once rose as far as the road after a typhoon. I watched from a second-floor window as a blue bucket floated away along the road. After that, the town built a high wall along the river. It was in order to keep the water out. Thanks to it, the water no longer rises even in sudden rain.
But since the wall went up, the river cannot be seen from the town. You can hear the sound of the wind, yet the surface of the water is not visible. The small waves that rise on a windy day can no longer be seen either. We have lost the surface of the water shining silver.
Now a narrow walkway has been built on top of the wall, so that you can see the river as you walk. According to the person who manages it, there was a long discussion over whether to build it. In the evenings, people from the neighbourhood talk amiably on the walkway. Safety, or a life with the water in view. Make it a matter of choosing one of the two and no answer comes. Looking for a form that satisfies both a little seems to work better, anywhere in the world.
The river water still cannot be drunk. Even so, being a town with the water in view matters to me.
